article.title: Route across providers with priority and weight
article.excerpt: Bind a key to more than one provider and the platform becomes the routing layer — balancing load when all is well, failing over when it is not.

p: Routing is controlled by two independent numbers on each channel. They answer different questions, which is why using only one of them cannot express both common setups.

head: Dial
What it decides
When it acts
rows: Which channel takes over when another fails
How traffic is split while all channels are healthy

p2: The distinction is deliberate: weight alone cannot express "keep the backup idle until the primary breaks", and priority alone cannot express "send three for every one".

list: All weights equal → ordered failover. The lowest priority number is tried first and the rest stand by until it fails.
Weights not all equal → smooth weighted round-robin, so the split follows the weight ratio, with the remaining channels covering failures.
sections.note: The send response and every receipt name the provider that actually carried the message, so reconciliation never depends on guessing which channel was used.

steps.p: Channels → Add connection, one per provider account you want in the rotation.
A single API key can send over several channels. This is what puts the platform in the routing path.
Give each channel its failover order and its share of healthy traffic.
Read the provider field in the response — it tells you which channel carried the message.

sections.h: Sender numbers rotate inside a channel too
p: A channel's sender numbers are expanded into virtual channels that join the same rotation, weighted by channel weight × sender weight. Rotating senders is how you work around a provider's per-number concurrency limit without changing your integration.
The rotation is transparent: you keep sending to the same endpoint, and the platform decides which number leaves the building.
